title: Polar operations, powers, and all roots
objective: Use polar multiplication, division, and integer powers, recover all distinct low-order roots, and choose rectangular addition when polar angles cannot be added directly.
why: Multiplication and powers become simpler when size and direction are separated. Complete root sets also explain why one inverse operation can have several answers. These skills prepare later phasor and signal work without assuming a circuit model.

prerequisites.label: Polar coordinates, arguments, and Euler form

sections.heading: Quick recall
paragraphs: In polar multiplication, multiply magnitudes and add angles. In division by a nonzero value, divide magnitudes and subtract angles. For integer n and nonzero z, $(re^{i\theta})^n=r^ne^{in\theta}$; normalize the final angle only when a principal representative is requested.
For w=ρe^(iθ)≠0, its nth roots are $\rho^{1/n}e^{i(\theta+2\pi k)/n}$ for k=0,…,n-1. These are n distinct points. Zero has just one distinct nth root, zero. Addition uses rectangular components.

sections.heading: Rotation and scale explain the product rule
paragraphs: The complex exponential obeys e^(iα)e^(iβ)=e^(i(α+β)). Multiplying by a complex number therefore combines a scale change and a rotation. Multiplying two radii gives the new radius, and the two turns add.

Division reverses those effects. Dividing by se^(iβ), with s>0, scales by 1/s and rotates by -β. A negative angle is a clockwise turn, so subtracting a negative argument adds a counterclockwise turn. Keep the operation and parentheses visible until the arithmetic is finished.

sections.heading: Integer powers include reciprocal cases
paragraphs: Repeated multiplication gives the positive-integer power rule. For a negative integer, first recall that z^(-n)=1/z^n. The radius is inverted and the angle reverses sign as the power changes sign.

For nonzero z, z^0=1. Zero has positive powers, but it has no reciprocal and therefore no negative integer powers. This refresher does not assign a value to 0^0; any zeroth-power exercise explicitly uses a nonzero base.

sections.heading: All roots come from all full-turn representatives
paragraphs: Suppose z^n=w and w≠0. Its root magnitude must be ρ^(1/n), because raising that radius to n must give ρ. Its angle must satisfy nφ=θ+2πk. Dividing by n gives φ=(θ+2πk)/n.

Taking k from 0 to n-1 yields n distinct points separated by 2π/n. The next k repeats the first direction after a full turn. Using only θ/n misses the other roots; using more than n successive values repeats them. Verify each proposed root by raising it to the requested power.

sections.heading: Root sets and zero need explicit interpretation
paragraphs: A principal square root is one chosen value. Solving z²=w asks for all solutions, which include both signs when w≠0. For a negative real target, the principal square root has positive imaginary part, while its negative is the other solution.

The equation z^n=0 has one distinct solution, z=0. Algebraically that zero has multiplicity n, but it is still one point and one entry in a set of distinct roots. Do not count angle descriptions at radius zero as different solutions.

sections.heading: Addition needs a different representation
paragraphs: No general addition rule adds polar magnitudes and angles. Convert each addend to a+bi and combine coordinates. Opposing values can cancel even though each original magnitude is positive.

Choose the form that exposes the operation: rectangular form supports addition and subtraction, while polar form supports products, quotients, and powers. Later circuit courses add physical definitions for phasors and impedance. This refresher develops the complex arithmetic, not those physical models.

examples.title: Raise a rectangular value to a power

steps.reason: Equal positive components give a π/4 direction and radius √2.
The fourth power raises the radius and quadruples the angle.

examples.conclusion: A complex base can have a real power.

examples.title: Use a negative power

steps.reason: The negative exponent inverts the radius and reverses the rotation.
Euler's formula verifies the rectangular components.

examples.conclusion: Negative powers require a nonzero base.

examples.title: Distinguish the principal square root

steps.reason: The root radius is 3 and the two angles differ by π.
Both solve the equation, but the principal square root is the positive-imaginary one.

examples.conclusion: Type both values when the field asks for a root set.

examples.title: Three roots of a positive real

steps.reason: The root radius is 2 and the directions are 0, 2π/3, and 4π/3.
Convert all three directions into exact rectangular values.
Cubing verifies every candidate at once.

examples.conclusion: A positive real number has nonreal cube roots as well as its real cube root.

examples.title: Four roots of a negative real

steps.reason: The initial angle π is divided by 4, and adjacent roots differ by π/2.
Each direction has component magnitudes √2.
The fourth power verifies the target and the four distinct points exhaust the roots.

examples.conclusion: All sign combinations appear in this particular example.

examples.title: Let components cancel

steps.reason: Convert each addend separately.
The imaginary components cancel exactly.

examples.conclusion: Adding the radii and angles would incorrectly give 4.

examples.title: Count distinct zero roots
examples.prompt: Solve z^4=0 and report distinct roots and multiplicity.

steps.reason: A nonzero radius could not have a zero fourth power.
Four repeated polynomial factors produce one distinct value.

examples.conclusion: Enter zero once in the root set.

interaction.prompt: Choose a root order, root radius, and positive or negative real target. Predict every distinct complex root and the count; reveal evenly spaced points and a power-back table. Test zero separately from nonzero root circles.

summary: Polar products add angles; quotients subtract angles and need a nonzero divisor.
Integer powers act on radius and angle; negative powers need a nonzero base.
Include every distinct root and distinguish that set from a principal square root.
Use rectangular components for addition and cancellation.
